identity.title: Focused infection-source exam (line/exit sites, skin, abdomen, joints, sacrum, urine catheter)

technique.how: Undress and inspect every line, dialysis and drain/exit site (erythema, purulence, tunnel tenderness), all skin including back, sacrum, heels, perineum, injection sites and wounds; palpate abdomen (peritonism, Murphy sign, flank tenderness), joints and spine for warmth/effusion/tenderness; check urinary catheter, mouth, sinuses, ears and chest. Repeat daily while the source is unknown.
technique.prerequisites: Full exposure with dressings taken down, adequate lighting and analgesia; review lines, catheters and devices with their insertion dates; log-roll immobile patients to view the sacrum.
technique.contraindications: None; do not delay cultures and antibiotics in suspected sepsis while completing the survey.

interpretation.positive_finding: Purulence, spreading erythema or tunnel tenderness at a line/exit site, cellulitis or crepitus, a hot swollen joint, peritonism or flank tenderness, or a sacral/heel ulcer with surrounding infection identifies a probable source and directs cultures, source control and empiric therapy.
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal survey does not exclude an occult source: insertion-site inflammation is absent in nearly all catheter-related bloodstream infections, and intra-abdominal, urinary, endovascular and spinal infections are frequently silent in elderly, immunosuppressed or sedated patients.
interpretation.pitfalls: Line-site appearance has near-zero sensitivity for CRBSI (coagulase-negative staphylococci cause little inflammation); steroids, neutropenia and neuropathy blunt local signs; dressings, obesity and immobility hide sacral, perineal and injection-site infections. Pain out of proportion with unimpressive skin findings suggests necrotizing infection.
interpretation.changes_what: A positive survey targets cultures, imaging and source control (line removal, drainage, debridement); a negative survey mandates blood/urine cultures and imaging rather than reassurance.

sources.citation: Mermel LA, Allon M, Bouza E, Craven DE, et al. Clinical practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of intravascular catheter-related infection: 2009 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Clin Infect Dis. 2009.
Safdar N, Maki DG. Inflammation at the insertion site is not predictive of catheter-related bloodstream infection with short-term, noncuffed central venous catheters. Crit Care Med. 2002.

Seymour CW, Liu VX, Iwashyna TJ, Brunkhorst FM, et al. Assessment of Clinical Criteria for Sepsis: For the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA. 2016.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Never let a negative source survey withhold cultures, empiric antibiotics or imaging in a hypotensive, febrile or acutely confused patient with suspected infection.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis or pain out of proportion (necrotizing fasciitis), a hot joint, peritonism, or purulence at a central line/dialysis catheter in a septic patient require immediate surgical/source-control and line removal decisions.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No inter-observer data for the composite survey; Safdar & Maki scored site inflammation (pain, erythema, swelling, purulence) daily by research nurses, and most sites 'showed little or no inflammation at the time of removal' (Abstract, Results).

extraction_notes: A composite 'source survey' has no diagnostic-accuracy literature; only the line-site component is quantified, and only as a range. Safdar & Maki 2002 (1,263 noncuffed CVCs, mostly ICU, DNA-subtyping-confirmed CRBSI in 35): 'The sensitivity of local inflammation for diagnosis of CVC-related BSI was dismal (0-3%).' (Abstract, Results). Because this is a range rather than a point estimate it is not entered in estimates[] (RANGES rule); no specificity was reported. The IDSA 2009 guideline (Mermel) endorses that site inflammation is insensitive and that clinical findings are unreliable for CRBSI diagnosis (unverified recall of wording; PubMed abstract is a two-sentence summary). Seymour 2016 (qSOFA) is cited as context for sepsis screening, not for source identification. Status not_quantified.
